fixes.explanation: Simon of Cyrene, a man coming in from the country, gets the cross put on him to carry behind Jesus. Luke says the soldiers seized him. I think Simon woke up that morning with a totally different to-do list. Some days just grab you by the collar, friend.

Jesus turns to these women, the daughters of Jerusalem, and says, “…do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.” Think about that. He's on His way to the cross, and He's still the one looking out for them. Then He goes on to warn them about days that are coming. He sure doesn't brush them off.

The women who followed Jesus from Galilee show up at the very end of the passage, standing at a distance. Here, though, Jesus tells the weeping women, “…weep for yourselves and for your children.” That's who He names, friend.

Jesus says, “Blessed are the barren women, the wombs that never bore, and breasts that never nursed!” That's what people will say in the days He warns about. It's a strange thing to hear, and I think it tells us how heavy those days will be. He goes on to say people will call on the mountains and hills to fall on them and cover them.

You'd expect people to call that foolish, but Jesus says the opposite. He says people will declare, “Blessed are the barren women, the wombs that never bore, and breasts that never nursed!” That's flipped upside down from what we'd guess. That's what makes the warning stop you in your tracks.
Easy guess to make, friend, but Luke doesn't call these two disciples. He calls them criminals, led away to be executed with Jesus. Later in the passage, one of these two criminals has a lot to say.

Right, Luke calls them criminals, not disciples. He says, “Two others, who were criminals, were also led away to be executed with Jesus.” So Jesus isn't the only one led away. And hold onto those two, because one of them ends up in a conversation you won't forget.

Luke doesn't mention any hill or anybody being placed behind Him. He says the criminals were crucified there with Jesus, one on His right and the other on His left. That puts one on each side of Him, and that matters later when one of them speaks up.

Close, because both are crucified along with Him. But Luke says one is on His right and the other on His left. Not both on one side. One criminal on each side, and both of them end up speaking before this is over.

Luke doesn't record Jesus asking for that. What He says is, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” He asks forgiveness for them, not rescue for Himself. I think that's worth sitting with.

Jerusalem does come up in this passage, when Jesus speaks to the daughters of Jerusalem, but it's not the promise. He says, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.” Paradise is the word. And He says today.

Luke says the veil of the temple was torn down the middle. He puts it in the same verse as the sun being darkened. Luke doesn't explain what it means in this passage, so I won't guess. I'll just say it's a big moment.

Luke says the centurion saw what happened and “…gave glory to God…” He's a Roman army officer, and he's standing at a crucifixion. Then he says, “Surely this was a righteous man.” I think that's a real surprise.

Cheering isn't what Luke records, friend. He says the people who gathered “…returned home beating their breasts.” I think that tells us the day hit them hard. That's a very different trip home from a cheering one.

Right, it's not cheering. Luke says that when the people who had gathered saw what happened, “…they returned home beating their breasts.” I think it shows they walked home shaken. Luke doesn't say more about what was going through their minds.
